title: A Fire Tornado Hit Their Neighborhood. This Is All That’s Left.
byline: By Jose A. Del Real, Niko Koppel, Karthik Patanjali, Yuliya Parshina-Kottas, Benjamin Wilhelm, Evan Grothjan, Miles Peyton, Veda Shastri, Tim Chaffee and Jon Huang

contentUnits.title: A fire tornado in Redding
contentUnits.text:
A Fire Tornado Hit Their Neighborhood. This Is All That’s Left.

By Jose A. Del Real, Niko Koppel, Karthik Patanjali, Yuliya Parshina-Kottas, Benjamin Wilhelm, Evan Grothjan, Miles Peyton, Veda Shastri, Tim Chaffee and Jon Huang

The devastating Carr Fire continues to burn through parts of Northern California. We visited the town of Redding, where the high winds and flames left some areas barely recognizable. Examine the damage using augmented reality.

lifecycle.readerAction: Begin with the headline and lead before advancing into the neighborhood sequence.
lifecycle.visualFocus: The viewer faces a quiet reconstruction space with the story image, the AR cover and the chimney model establishing the damage-first frame.
lifecycle.sourceTextPreservation: Headline, byline and article lead are preserved from the captured HTML metadata.

contentUnits.title: The Carr Fire reaches Redding
contentUnits.text:
The Carr Fire has scorched Northern California with singular intensity since it broke out on July 23, displacing thousands of people in Shasta County and decimating parts of the bucolic town of Redding.

The fire took a particularly nightmarish turn when what locals are calling a fire tornado, documented in video footage and first-person accounts, tore through neighborhoods in the town of Redding, which has a population of more than 90,000.

lifecycle.readerAction: Compare the first neighborhood image pair while the article establishes the fire's arrival.
lifecycle.visualFocus: The floor route moves from Redding toward the fire-tornado marker while the first before/after pair appears.
lifecycle.sourceTextPreservation: The first two body paragraphs are grouped without rewriting.

contentUnits.title: Winds powerful enough to remake the ground
contentUnits.text:
Powerful winds pulled trees out of the ground, flung cars and engulfed nearby buildings in flames. All that was left were petrified trees and hollowed out homes. In some areas, the heat and wind grew so intense that there is no more soil on the ground, just charred bedrock. The winds, according to the National Weather Service, reached speeds “in excess of 143 miles per hour.”

The Carr Fire is still burning and it is only 41 percent contained, shifting westward from Redding. Residents are now slowly being allowed to return and assess the damage. Some have lost everything.

lifecycle.readerAction: Hold position and connect the wind description to the stripped neighborhood views.
lifecycle.visualFocus: The second before/after pair replaces the first as the slide model waits on the central plinth.
lifecycle.sourceTextPreservation: The wind, charred-bedrock and containment paragraphs are preserved as a single causal beat.

contentUnits.title: A neighborhood barely recognizable
contentUnits.text:
The scale of the destruction is hard to comprehend. Nearly 40,000 people were forced to evacuate their homes at the height of the wildfire's assault on Redding. It has burned more than 142,000 acres of land, destroying 1,073 homes and damaging an additional 190. Six fatalities have been reported, though that number could rise once a complete assessment of the damage can be conducted.

The Lake Keswick Estates area, among the very worst hit in Redding, is barely recognizable. All that is left in some homes are burned out refrigerators, washing machines and bed frames.

The remains of a row of houses on Menlo Way, a street in the Lake Keswick Estates area, which was devastated by the Carr fire.

lifecycle.readerAction: Use the captioned Menlo Way context to place the object models inside the broader neighborhood damage.
lifecycle.visualFocus: A third before/after pair surrounds the viewer while the bed frame appears as the first domestic remnant.
lifecycle.sourceTextPreservation: The evacuation, acreage, destroyed-home figures, Lake Keswick paragraph and captured caption are preserved.

contentUnits.title: A bed frame in the aftermath
contentUnits.text:
Rotate the bed to investigate the fire’s aftermath.

Outside many homes, in backyards and driveways, a few trappings of domestic life survived. A complete patio set, a swimming pool, a basketball hoop. Tattered, charred American flags sat stiffly in the former entryways of several homes. The homes themselves were largely gone. The heat from the fire was enough to melt a children’s slide.

lifecycle.readerAction: Inspect the bed frame as the source prompt and domestic-life paragraph are read together.
lifecycle.visualFocus: The bed GLB is isolated at arm's length, with domestic remains imagery and the Menlo Way view on either side.
lifecycle.sourceTextPreservation: The exact bed WebGL annotation is preserved, followed by the paragraph about domestic objects and a melted children's slide.

contentUnits.title: A slide distorted by heat
contentUnits.text:
Rotate the slide to explore the damage.

Justin Sanchez, who lives in the Lake Keswick Estates area, said that his neighbors had been on edge in the days before the fire. Many packed their belongings and watched weather reports obsessively, he said. But Mr. Sanchez didn't think the fire would reach his house. “None of us would have ever thought it would jump the river and come this way,” he said.

On the day the fire hit the town, he said, nobody could have anticipated its force. “It was this massive tornado headed straight for our neighborhood packed in with shrapnel flying around,” he said. “Within a matter of 10 minutes or so it was right on the edge of my neighborhood.”

lifecycle.readerAction: Compare the damaged slide with Justin Sanchez's account of the fire moving toward the neighborhood.
lifecycle.visualFocus: The slide replaces the bed while the first before/after pair returns to connect the quote to the neighborhood.
lifecycle.sourceTextPreservation: The exact slide WebGL annotation is preserved with the two Sanchez setup paragraphs.

contentUnits.title: Ten minutes at the edge of the neighborhood
contentUnits.text:
The evacuation was chaotic, he said. The bottlenecked traffic exacerbated his family’s panic. At one point, they feared they would not make it out alive.

When Mr. Sanchez returned on Thursday, one week after the evacuation, his entire home had been reduced to rubble.

lifecycle.readerAction: Stay seated as the route, rather than the camera, carries the story through evacuation and return.
lifecycle.visualFocus: The floor marker advances toward the return point while the slide remains as evidence of heat and speed.
lifecycle.sourceTextPreservation: The chaotic-evacuation and return-to-rubble paragraphs are preserved together.

contentUnits.title: The chimney still standing
contentUnits.text:
Rotate the chimney. This was the only part of the home left standing.

In the moments before his family evacuated, Mr. Sanchez began pulling photos off the walls and loading them into his dad’s truck. The force of the wind, he said, blew them out of his hands. He jumped in the back of the truck, laying on top of the pictures to keep them from flying away.

Today, that's all they have left.

“I just knew this thing was going to take our whole neighborhood,” he said. “I’ve never been so scared in my life.”

lifecycle.readerAction: Inspect the chimney while the text narrows from neighborhood scale to what one family carried out.
lifecycle.visualFocus: The chimney model becomes the final AR object, framed by before/after imagery and the personal account of saved photographs.
lifecycle.sourceTextPreservation: The exact chimney WebGL annotation and the three paragraphs about photos, loss and fear are preserved.

contentUnits.title: Day by day
contentUnits.text: Mr. Sanchez, who has been staying in a motel with his family, including two children, said he’s not sure what comes next. “It’s going to be chaotic. We’re just going to have to work through it,” he said. “We just have to take it day by day.”

lifecycle.readerAction: End with the uncertainty of what comes next rather than a spectacle of the fire itself.
lifecycle.visualFocus: The route resolves at the return marker and the chimney stays centered as the final unresolved object.
lifecycle.sourceTextPreservation: The final Sanchez paragraph is preserved as the closing beat.
